criteria.evidence: The implementation lacks all three key components required by the criterion: (1) IP-based tracking—the code accepts only an attempt count with no IP awareness, (2) time windowing—no timestamp or 15-minute expiry logic exists, and (3) HTTP endpoint integration—the code is a plain function, not a POST handler. While npm test passes, it only validates a numeric threshold (login(6)→429), not the actual rate-limiting behavior specified.

data.quality_reason: Code is syntactically correct and executes, but is a placeholder rather than a real implementation. It lacks all infrastructure for genuine rate limiting: no IP tracking, no time management, no state persistence, no HTTP integration, and no attempt to handle authentication state. The implementation is overly simplistic and disconnected from the actual requirement.
data.verdict_reason: The criterion requires IP-based rate limiting over a 15-minute window on a POST endpoint, but the implementation provides only a simple numeric threshold check. The test passes because it validates the wrong thing—a unit test of internal logic rather than verification of the stated requirement. The code is a non-functional stub that ignores all spatial (IP) and temporal (15-minute window) constraints specified in c1.
recommendations: Store failed attempts per IP address using a Map or persistent store (Redis/database) keyed by client IP, with attempt count and timestamp.
Implement a 15-minute sliding window by checking timestamps; decrement counters or clear entries older than 15 minutes, and increment only on fresh attempts within the window.
Integrate the rate limiter as middleware in an HTTP framework (Express, etc.) to extract client IP from requests and coordinate with login authentication to track only actual failed attempts.
